record.label: Finite Gaussian maximizers are unique up to reversal
record.statement: For every fixed positive integer n, the pure zero-field SK Hamiltonian with independent standard Gaussian pair couplings has almost surely exactly one maximizing pair {sigma,-sigma}. Configurations not related by global reversal differ in at least one pair product, so their energy difference is a nondegenerate Gaussian; a finite union excludes all such ties. This does not exclude nearly maximizing configurations at other overlaps in the large-n limit.
record.boundary: Elementary finite-model deduction. It distinguishes exact maximizers at fixed size from near-ground pairs and supplies no rate, algorithm, formal replay or independent acceptance.

aligned_passages.text: Choose one minimizer supplied by the attained Parisi formula, and apply the full-support theorem to that same coefficient. The external landscape theorem below then applies at every point of its Stieltjes support. For every fixed $r\in[0,1)$ and $\varepsilon,\eta>0$, there is a constant $K=K(r,\varepsilon,\eta)>0$, independent of $n$, such that $$ \mathbb P\left(\exists\sigma,\tau\in\{-1,1\}^n: \left|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i\tau_i-r\right|<\varepsilon, \quad \frac{H_n(\sigma)}n,\frac{H_n(\tau)}n\ge P_*-\eta\right) \ge1-Ke^{-n/K},\qquad n\ge1. $$ The probability is over the SK couplings; the configurations may depend on them. This is the specialization of [Auffinger–Chen–Zeng, Proposition 1, equation (5), p. 5][acz] to the full-support minimizer above. Their theorem applies to each point of its Stieltjes support. Its proof, on pp. 15–16, uses the coupled free energy constrained to a neighbourhood of that overlap, passes to the coupled maximum and applies Gaussian concentration. The coupled maximum approaches $2P_*$, while the unrestricted maximum approaches $P_*$; these two facts force both members of a maximizing pair to be near ground energy. The covariance normalization needs one small adjustment. Writing $R=n^{-1}\sum_i\sigma_i\tau_i$, our Hamiltonian has covariance $nR^2/2-1/2$. Adjoin a common independent Gaussian $C$ of variance $1/2$. Then $\widetilde H_n(\sigma)=H_n(\sigma)+C$ has covariance $n\xi(R)$ with $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, as in the cited mixed-spin theorem. Its expected maximum equals that of $H_n$, so its ground-state limit is the same $P_*$. Apply the theorem with energy tolerance $\eta/2$. On $|C|\le\eta n/2$, the resulting pair also satisfies the displayed energy inequalities for $H_n$. The omitted event has probability at most $2e^{-\eta^2n^2/4}$, which can be absorbed into $Ke^{-n/K}$ by enlarging $K$. Since the conclusion for $H_n$ depends only on its couplings, this also removes the auxiliary Gaussian from the probability statement. The pointwise result also gives a simultaneous statement at any fixed positive resolution. Given $\varepsilon,\eta>0$, choose finitely many centres $r_j\in[0,1)$ whose open $\varepsilon/2$-neighbourhoods cover $[0,1]$. Apply the preceding result at each centre with overlap tolerance $\varepsilon/2$ and energy tolerance $\eta$. A finite union bound gives constants $C,c>0$, depending only on these tolerances, such that $$ \mathbb P\!\left(\forall r\in[-1,1]\ \exists\sigma,\tau\in\{-1,1\}^n: |R(\sigma,\tau)-r|<\varepsilon,\quad H_n(\sigma)/n,H_n(\tau)/n\ge P_*-\eta\right) \ge1-Ce^{-cn}. \tag{9.1} $$ Indeed, on the event where every centre has a suitable pair, choose a nearest centre and use the triangle inequality. ## 6. Return to the spins At a fixed finite size, almost surely the only exact maximisers are a configuration and its global reversal. Indeed, two configurations that are neither equal nor global reversals differ in some pair product. Their energy difference is then a Gaussian with positive variance, so a tie has probability zero; there are only finitely many pairs. Intermediate separations become possible when we allow a small loss per spin and let the system grow. A separate theorem of [Auffinger–Chen–Zeng, Proposition 1, equation (5)][acz] applies at each point in the minimiser's support. Combining it with full support: for every fixed overlap $r\in[0,1)$ and tolerances $\varepsilon,\eta>0$, with probability over the couplings tending to one exponentially fast as $n\to\infty$, there exist configurations $\sigma,\tau$ with $$ |R(\sigma,\tau)-r|<\varepsilon, \qquad H_n(\sigma)/n,\ H_n(\tau)/n\ge P_*-\eta. $$ If $k$ sites differ, $k/n=(1-R)/2$. The overlap tolerance therefore gives $$ \left|\frac{k}{n}-\frac{1-r}{2}\right|<\frac\varepsilon2. $$ For example, fix an energy loss $\eta>0$ per spin and take $r=1/2$ and $\varepsilon=0.02$. With probability tending to one exponentially fast, the same instance has two configurations with energies per spin at least $P_*-\eta$ and a differing-site fraction between $0.24$ and $0.26$. No numerical threshold for $n$ is asserted. At target zero, the differing-site fraction can be arbitrarily close to one half. The pair may depend on the chosen target and the couplings. This is existence for each fixed target, not a statement about typically sampled pairs or a procedure for finding them. The companion *Long Reasoning Record*, [§9.3, “Near-ground configurations at a prescribed overlap”](../long/reasoning-record.md#near-ground-overlaps), gives the probability bound, covariance adjustment and exact finite-size comparison. The threshold $P_*-\eta$ refers to the limiting value, whereas an exact maximiser attains its particular finite instance's maximum. **Question 5: use the spin conclusion.** Fix an energy loss $\eta>0$. How can the theorem give two configurations differing on between 69% and 71% of sites, although it is stated for nonnegative overlap targets? Which earlier symmetry is needed? Does the stated theorem also permit the choice $\eta=1/n$? [Answer 5](#answer-5).
